cards.front: What general rule describes how lipids control the location of signaling proteins at membranes?
cards.back: Lipids control signaling protein location by supplying grip, address, or both.
cards.why: Grip is a covalent anchor or charge patch on the protein; address is a lipid on the membrane, such as PIP3, that a protein domain reads.
cards.quote: Lipids control signaling protein location by supplying grip, address, or both.

cards.front: Myristate is attached through an amide bond to an {{c1::N-terminal glycine}}, usually while the protein is still being made.
cards.quote: Myristate goes on a glycine that becomes the first residue after the starting methionine is clipped off, usually while the protein is still being made.
cards.section: Covalent anchors: what is attached, and where?

cards.front: Of myristate, palmitate, farnesyl and geranylgeranyl, which anchor is readily removed from a protein, and what enzymes remove it?
cards.back: Palmitate, attached to a cysteine by a thioester, is removed by thioesterases. The other three are essentially permanent.
cards.quote: only palmitate's thioester is readily hydrolyzed, by thioesterases.
cards.section: Covalent anchors: what is attached, and where?

cards.front: After a CAAX-box cysteine is prenylated, what happens to the C-terminal end of the protein?
cards.back: The last three residues are removed and the new end is methylated, hiding its charge.
cards.quote: After prenylation, the last three residues are removed and the new end is methylated, hiding its charge.
cards.section: Covalent anchors: what is attached, and where?

cards.front: Prenyl groups contain five-carbon isoprene units: {{c1::three}} in farnesyl and four in geranylgeranyl.
cards.quote: Prenyl groups contain five-carbon isoprene units: three in farnesyl and four in geranylgeranyl.
cards.section: Covalent anchors: what is attached, and where?

cards.front: Cells are pulse-labelled with radioactive palmitate, then chased with excess unlabeled palmitate. The label on protein Y halves every 15 minutes, while a separate amino-acid pulse-chase shows Y itself lasts many hours. What fraction of the starting label remains after 60 minutes, and what does this show?
cards.back: 6.25%. 60 min is 4 half-lives, so (1/2)^4 = 1/16. Palmitate is being removed and replaced on a stable protein.
cards.why: Only palmitate's thioester is readily hydrolyzed; the protein itself is not turning over.
cards.quote: only palmitate's thioester is readily hydrolyzed, by thioesterases.
cards.section: Covalent anchors: what is attached, and where?

cards.front: A signaling protein's only membrane attachment is a single myristate on its N-terminal glycine. How well will it stay on membranes, and what would make its residence lasting?
cards.back: It will associate with membranes only weakly and come off again. A second contact, such as palmitate or a patch of positive charge, makes residence strong.
cards.why: Fyn and Lck pair myristate with palmitate; one anchor is usually not enough.
cards.quote: The first film's Ras pairings are not the only ones: Fyn and Lck carry myristate plus palmitate.
cards.section: Two contacts make residence strong and regulatable

cards.front: At body temperature, about how much extra favourable free energy changes a binding equilibrium by about tenfold?
cards.back: About 1.4 kcal/mol. The exact gain from a second contact depends on geometry and local concentration.
cards.quote: At body temperature, an extra favourable contribution of about 1.4 kcal/mol changes the equilibrium by about tenfold.
cards.section: Two contacts make residence strong and regulatable

cards.front: K-Ras4B has a farnesyl group and a run of lysines. Protein kinase C phosphorylates Ser181 beside the lysines. Why does this tend to release K-Ras4B from the plasma membrane?
cards.back: The phosphate adds negative charge beside the lysines, weakening their attraction to the membrane, so K-Ras4B tends to move to internal membranes.
cards.why: This is a farnesyl-electrostatic switch: removing one of two contacts releases the protein.
cards.quote: The added negative charge weakens attraction to the plasma membrane, so K-Ras4B tends to move to internal membranes, including mitochondrial membranes.
cards.section: Two contacts make residence strong and regulatable

cards.front: What does PDEδ do for a farnesylated Ras protein?
cards.back: PDEδ has a hydrophobic pocket that shields the farnesyl group and helps Ras cross the cytosol between membranes.
cards.quote: PDEδ, a carrier with a hydrophobic pocket, can shield a farnesyl group and help Ras cross the cytosol between membranes.
cards.section: Two contacts make residence strong and regulatable

cards.front: Where does palmitate go on H-Ras and where can it come off, and what does removal do to H-Ras?
cards.back: It goes on mainly at the Golgi and can come off anywhere. Removal weakens the grip, so H-Ras samples internal membranes and returns toward the Golgi for another round.
cards.quote: Thioesterases can remove palmitate wherever H-Ras sits, which weakens its grip and lets it sample internal membranes and return toward the Golgi for another round.
cards.section: Palmitate turns a hold into a cycle

cards.front: What is a kinetic bilayer trap, and does it need a plasma-membrane-specific receptor for H-Ras?
cards.back: Steady-state enrichment created by the rates of trapping, vesicle transport, release and recapture. No plasma-membrane-specific receptor is required.
cards.quote: No plasma-membrane-specific receptor for H-Ras is required: the rates of trapping, vesicle transport, release and recapture create steady-state enrichment.
cards.section: Palmitate turns a hold into a cycle

cards.front: A drug blocks the thioesterase that removes palmitate from H-Ras. Does H-Ras become soluble, tighten at the plasma membrane, or lose its focused distribution?
cards.back: It loses its focused distribution and spreads across membranes. It is not soluble, because palmitate still binds it to membrane.
cards.why: Without release, return and recapture at the Golgi, the cycle that maintains plasma-membrane enrichment stalls.
cards.quote: Palmitate still provides membrane binding, so H-Ras does not become soluble.
cards.section: Palmitate turns a hold into a cycle

cards.front: GFP-H-Ras is 85% in the membrane fraction. Changing the CAAX cysteine to serine gives 6%; changing the two palmitoylated cysteines to serine gives 35%; GFP alone gives 5%. What do these data show about the two anchors?
cards.back: The CAAX cysteine (prenylation) is needed for essentially any membrane binding, since its loss is near GFP alone. Palmitoylation adds strength, since its loss lowers but does not abolish binding.
cards.why: The CAAX cysteine carries the first lipid; palmitate is a second contact.
cards.quote: A CAAX box is a cysteine, two aliphatic amino acids and a final residue that helps determine which prenyltransferase acts.
cards.section: Covalent anchors: what is attached, and where?

cards.front: A farnesyltransferase inhibitor is given to cells for a day. Does it remove farnesyl from Ras that already has it?
cards.back: No. It keeps newly made Ras from acquiring its farnesyl grip; farnesyl already attached stays on.
cards.quote: An FTI keeps newly made Ras from acquiring its farnesyl grip; it does not strip farnesyl that is already attached.
cards.section: Can blocking an anchor block cancer signaling?

cards.front: Why can a farnesyltransferase inhibitor fail to move K-Ras and N-Ras off the membrane but still work on H-Ras?
cards.back: K-Ras and N-Ras can receive geranylgeranyl on the same CAAX cysteine and stay membrane-associated. H-Ras is not rescued this way.
cards.why: This backup helps explain why FTIs disappointed against K-Ras, the most commonly mutated Ras gene.
cards.quote: K-Ras and N-Ras can receive geranylgeranyl on the same CAAX cysteine and remain membrane-associated; H-Ras is not rescued this way.
cards.section: Can blocking an anchor block cancer signaling?

cards.front: With an FTI alone, plasma-membrane GFP-H-Ras falls from 90% to 10% and K-Ras4B from 80% to 74%. FTI plus a geranylgeranyltransferase I inhibitor drops K-Ras4B to 14%. What observation pattern supports a backup anchor for K-Ras4B?
cards.back: K-Ras4B localization falls only when both prenyltransferases are inhibited, while H-Ras falls with the FTI alone. That supports geranylgeranylation as a backup for K-Ras4B but not H-Ras.
cards.quote: Membrane localization that falls only when both prenyltransferases are inhibited supports a backup enzyme.
cards.section: Can blocking an anchor block cancer signaling?

cards.front: In cells, Ser181 of K-Ras4B is changed to alanine, which cannot be phosphorylated, and protein kinase C is then activated. How does the mutant's distribution compare with normal K-Ras4B, and why?
cards.back: The mutant should stay largely at the plasma membrane, as the switch predicts, while normal K-Ras4B tends to move to internal membranes. It cannot gain the negative charge that weakens the lysine patch's attraction to the membrane.
cards.why: Rests on the farnesyl-electrostatic switch: kinase-added negative charge beside the lysines is what releases the protein.
cards.quote: The added negative charge weakens attraction to the plasma membrane, so K-Ras4B tends to move to internal membranes, including mitochondrial membranes.
cards.section: Two contacts make residence strong and regulatable

cards.front: A drug blocks the palmitoyl acyltransferase that works at the Golgi. Using only the lesson's rules, predict what happens to plasma-membrane enrichment of H-Ras, and why it differs from blocking the thioesterase.
cards.back: Enrichment should be largely lost (inferred from palmitate going on mainly at the Golgi). Without palmitate, H-Ras keeps only its farnesyl grip, which is weak, so it should not be trapped and carried to the plasma membrane. Blocking the thioesterase instead leaves palmitate on, so H-Ras stays membrane-bound but spreads out.
cards.why: Rests on: palmitate goes on mainly at the Golgi, and one anchor is usually not enough.
cards.quote: the robust point is that palmitate goes on mainly at the Golgi and can come off anywhere.
cards.section: Palmitate turns a hold into a cycle

cards.front: Which phosphoinositide is enriched at the Golgi, which on early endosomes, and which at the plasma membrane?
cards.back: PI4P at the Golgi, PI3P on early endosomes and PI(4,5)P2 (PIP2) at the plasma membrane.
cards.quote: They are enriched differently: PI4P at the Golgi, PI3P on early endosomes and PI(4,5)P2, called PIP2, at the plasma membrane.
cards.section: Phosphoinositides make dynamic addresses

cards.front: Class I PI3-kinase adds the 3-phosphate to {{c1::PIP2}} to make PI(3,4,5)P3, or PIP3.
cards.quote: The second film's writer is class I PI3-kinase, which adds the 3-phosphate to PIP2 to make PI(3,4,5)P3, or PIP3.
cards.section: Phosphoinositides make dynamic addresses

cards.front: A fluorescent reporter's PIP3-reading domain is replaced with one that selectively reads PI4P. Which compartment should look brightest, and what caveat applies?
cards.back: The Golgi, the classic PI4P-rich compartment. In practice sensitive PI4P probes also light up the plasma membrane and late endosomes. A reader's pattern reflects its ligand plus coincident contacts.
cards.quote: The expected answer is the Golgi, the classic PI4P-rich compartment.
cards.section: Phosphoinositides make dynamic addresses

cards.front: What is a PH domain, and does every PH domain read PIP3?
cards.back: A fold of roughly 100 amino acids. Only some have a pocket for a particular phosphoinositide head group, and many do not read PIP3. Akt's does.
cards.quote: Only some PH domains have a pocket for a particular phosphoinositide head group, and many do not read PIP3.
cards.section: Readers and erasers

cards.front: Which enzymes erase PIP3, and what does each remove?
cards.back: PTEN removes the 3-phosphate. SHIP1 and SHIP2 remove the 5-phosphate instead, producing PI(3,4)P2.
cards.quote: PTEN, which removes the 3-phosphate, is not the only eraser: SHIP1 and SHIP2 remove the 5-phosphate instead, producing PI(3,4)P2.
cards.section: Readers and erasers

cards.front: SHIP activity rises while PI3-kinase activity stays the same. Must Akt recruitment fall in direct proportion to PIP3?
cards.back: No. SHIP lowers PIP3 but makes PI(3,4)P2, which Akt's PH domain can still bind, so recruitment can outlast or differ from the PIP3 pattern.
cards.quote: Recruitment can therefore outlast or differ from the PIP3 pattern.
cards.section: Readers and erasers

cards.front: A PIP3-binding PH-domain-GFP reporter is cytosolic in resting, serum-starved normal cells. Where is it in otherwise identical cells with no working PTEN, and why?
cards.back: Largely at the plasma membrane even at rest. Without PTEN, PIP3 from basal PI3-kinase activity is not erased, so localization follows lipid level, not the stimulus alone.
cards.quote: Cells lacking PTEN should retain more membrane reporter even at rest, showing that localization follows lipid level, not the stimulus alone.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A growth factor recruits a PH-domain-GFP reporter to the plasma membrane. What do a pocket-mutant reporter and a PI3-kinase inhibitor such as wortmannin each show?
cards.back: The pocket mutant stays cytosolic, showing recruitment requires lipid binding. The inhibitor blocks recruitment, showing the lipid depends on PI3-kinase.
cards.quote: The pocket mutant should remain cytosolic after stimulation, showing that recruitment requires lipid binding.
cards.section: Turn recruitment into a measurement

cards.front: Design a reporter that lights up the plasma membrane only where and when PI3-kinase is active. What is the construct, and which controls show specificity?
cards.back: GFP fused to a PH domain that binds PIP3 tightly and selectively; the GRP1 PH domain is cleaner than Akt's, which also binds PI(3,4)P2. Controls: pocket mutant, PI3-kinase inhibitor, PTEN-null cells that keep more membrane reporter at rest, and a free red fluorescent protein.
cards.quote: Fuse GFP to a PH domain that binds PIP3 tightly and selectively.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why report a membrane green-to-red ratio, with a free red fluorescent protein, rather than green intensity alone?
cards.back: A thick membrane ruffle can brighten both channels without any chemical change. The ratio separates a real recruitment from a shape effect.
cards.quote: a thick ruffle can brighten both channels without any chemical change.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: SHIP is overexpressed while PI3-kinase activity is unchanged. Compare the membrane signal of a GRP1 PH-domain reporter with an Akt PH-domain reporter, and explain.
cards.back: The GRP1 reporter falls with PIP3. The Akt reporter falls less, because SHIP converts PIP3 to PI(3,4)P2, which Akt's PH domain can still bind.
cards.why: Rests on: SHIP removes the 5-phosphate making PI(3,4)P2; Akt's domain reads both lipids; a PIP3-preferring domain is cleaner.
cards.quote: SHIP lowers PIP3 but makes PI(3,4)P2, which Akt's PH domain can still bind.
cards.section: Readers and erasers

cards.front: Which two proteins must Ras meet at the membrane, and what does each do?
cards.back: SOS, the exchange factor that loads GTP, and Raf, the kinase that active Ras recruits. Grb2 recruits SOS to the membrane.
cards.quote: Ras must meet SOS, the exchange factor that loads GTP, and Raf, the kinase active Ras recruits.
cards.section: Why membrane location matters

cards.front: Why does being at a membrane help a signaling protein meet partners?
cards.back: A membrane reduces the search from three dimensions to two, raising encounter frequency for partners confined there.
cards.quote: A membrane reduces a search from three dimensions to two, raising encounter frequency for partners confined there.
cards.section: Why membrane location matters

cards.front: How does the inner face of the plasma membrane differ from the outer face and the Golgi, in terms of lipid charge?
cards.back: It is rich in negatively charged lipids, which helps attract patches of positive charge such as lysine runs.
cards.quote: The inner plasma-membrane face also differs from the outer face and the Golgi: it is rich in negatively charged lipids.
cards.section: Why membrane location matters

cards.front: What is the status of the idea that palmitoylated proteins sit in cholesterol-rich lipid rafts?
cards.back: Living membranes contain small, short-lived ordered domains, but their size, lifetime and importance for sorting particular proteins remain debated.
cards.quote: Living membranes contain small, short-lived ordered domains, but their size, lifetime and importance for sorting particular proteins remain debated.
cards.section: Rafts and reporter limits

cards.front: Besides PIP3 level, what else can a PH-domain reporter's membrane signal reflect?
cards.back: Other lipids, general charge and coincident protein contacts. Membrane shape also changes apparent intensity.
cards.quote: A PH-domain reporter can also reflect other lipids, general charge and coincident protein contacts.
cards.section: Rafts and reporter limits
